tier_reason: docs/data.txt is raw `go test -bench=.` output with the CPU model (i5-11400) comparing Encode/Decode against BenchmarkStdEncode/StdDecode (encoding/binary), and the benchmark code is public in varint_test.go; the Go version is not stated and the author warns the benchmark favours his code, so first-party C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/data.txt (i5-11400, go test -bench): encode at 63 bits 2.992 ns/op versus 5.051 ns/op for binary.PutUvarint (about 1.7x, derived from page data); decode at 63 bits 2.754 versus 5.510 ns/op (about 2.0x, derived from page data); encode+decode round trip at 63 bits 5.726 versus 8.256 ns/op. At 7 bits encode is a tie (0.6907 versus 0.6875 ns/op) and decode is slower than Uvarint (1.154 versus 0.9654 ns/op); the gap opens above 35 bits.
corrections.caveats: Go version not stated. Win is limited to values over about 35 bits; at 7 bits decode is about 20% slower than the standard library (not inlined), and encode at 14-35 bits is slightly slower. The README itself warns that the benchmark advantages chmike/varint through branch prediction because each run encodes values of a single magnitude. Uses a different wire format (big-endian prefix code), so it is not a drop-in replacement for LEB128 data. Marginal fit for the bitpacking category.
